chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
title: American musicians, Japanese big bands and jazz as an American product
summary: Wooding complains cabaret owners are too stingy to hire bands, compares Japan's large bands, and says jazz came from the melting pot but Black musicians created most of it.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Which, I wanted to say one thing here. The American musician is losing out, because the impresarios and the cabaret owners are too stingy to hire a band, but when we played -- when Miss Rae Ray Harrison and I played in Tokyo and all over Japan, they had bands that had eighteen pieces. And I know they don't have the money comparable to American cabaret goers and

theater goers. Now, they had everything there. Now, these boys are learning to play with big bands, while we are here -- the only thing that's saving the American musician against these foreign musicians, like in Japan, is because -- and some of the other Oriental countries -- is because they cannot im-provise, but they're good copyists. And they're good musicians. They can read and then they can copy a solo, an American solo, off the tape, or off the record. But they can't produce them themselves, yet. But, in time, that will come.

And then we'll be number two in bands, even with the stuff that we created. Because their jazz is an American product. I know that some people will say that 60% of it is black. But it still is an American product. And, you know, we're all, it's part of the melting pot. It came out of the melting pot where everybody contributed something to it. But we, we contributed the most part. That's why we feel that we should have a chance to work at it. Is because we have created the most of it and it was through us that it got started.
